title: Foundational Lemma: b mod (b-1) = 1
content: The key helper: for $b \geq 3$, $b \bmod (b-1) = 1$. Proved by rewriting $b = (b-1) + 1$ via `Nat.mod_eq_sub_mod`, then reducing to $1 \bmod (b-1) = 1$ by `Nat.mod_eq_of_lt`. This single fact drives the entire theory: $b^k \equiv 1^k = 1 \pmod{b-1}$, so digit sums preserve residues.
mathContext: $b \bmod (b-1) = ((b-1)+1) \bmod (b-1) = 1 \bmod (b-1) = 1$ since $1 < b-1$ for $b \geq 3$. Consequence: $n = \sum_i d_i b^i \equiv \sum_i d_i \cdot 1 = \sum_i d_i \pmod{b-1}$.

title: The Base-b Digital Root
content: Defines `digitalRootBase b n` directly via the closed form: 0 for $n = 0$, $1 + ((n-1) \bmod (b-1))$ for $n > 0$. The formula cycles through $\{1, 2, \ldots, b-1\}$ as $n$ increases, with $\text{dr}_b(k(b-1)) = b-1$ (not 0), matching the convention that the digital root of a positive multiple of $b-1$ is $b-1$ itself.

title: Core Congruence: n ≡ dr_b(n) (mod b-1)
content: The central theorem: $n \equiv \text{dr}_b(n) \pmod{b-1}$ for $b \geq 3$. Two proofs: (1) `digitSum_mod_base_pred` delegates to Mathlib's `Nat.modEq_digits_sum` for the digit sum version, and (2) `congruence` proves the closed-form version directly by rewriting $n = (n-1) + 1$ and applying `Nat.add_mod`. The `conv_lhs` tactic targets the left-hand side for rewriting.
mathContext: $n \bmod (b-1) = \text{dr}_b(n) \bmod (b-1)$. Since $\text{dr}_b(n) \in \{0, 1, \ldots, b-1\}$ and $b-1 \geq 2$, this means $\text{dr}_b(n)$ is the canonical representative of $n$ in $\mathbb{Z}/(b-1)\mathbb{Z}$ (with 0 mapped to $b-1$ for positive $n$).

title: Range, Fixed Points, and Idempotence
content: Three properties forming a logical chain: (1) **Range**: $1 \leq \text{dr}_b(n) \leq b-1$ for $n > 0$, from `Nat.mod_lt`. (2) **Fixed point**: single-digit numbers are fixed ($\text{dr}_b(n) = n$ for $1 \leq n \leq b-1$), from `Nat.mod_eq_of_lt`. (3) **Idempotence**: $\text{dr}_b(\text{dr}_b(n)) = \text{dr}_b(n)$, by composing range with fixed point. This chain illustrates how range analysis implies algebraic properties.
mathContext: $\text{dr}_b$ is an idempotent function (a retraction). The image $\{0, 1, \ldots, b-1\}$ is the set of fixed points. Algebraically, $\text{dr}_b$ is a projection from $(\mathbb{N}, +)$ onto $\mathbb{Z}/(b-1)\mathbb{Z}$ (shifted by 1 to avoid 0 for positive inputs).

title: Divisibility by (b-1) via Digital Root
content: Proves $(b-1) \mid n \iff \text{dr}_b(n) = b-1$ for $n > 0, b \geq 3$. The forward direction: if $n = k(b-1)$ with $k \geq 1$, then $n - 1 = (b-2) + (b-1)(k-1)$, so $(n-1) \bmod (b-1) = b-2$ and $\text{dr}_b(n) = b-1$. The reverse: if $\text{dr}_b(n) = b-1$, then $n \bmod (b-1) = (b-1) \bmod (b-1) = 0$ by the congruence theorem.
mathContext: $(b-1) \mid n \iff \text{dr}_b(n) = b-1$ for $n > 0$. In base 10: $9 \mid n \iff \text{dr}_{10}(n) = 9$. In base 16: $15 \mid n \iff \text{dr}_{16}(n) = 15$.

title: General Factor Divisibility Rule
content: The most powerful result: for any divisor $d \geq 2$ of $b-1$, we have $d \mid n \iff d \mid \text{digitSum}_b(n)$. The proof shows $b \bmod d = 1$ (since $d \mid (b-1)$ implies $b = dk + 1$ for some $k$), then applies Mathlib's `Nat.dvd_iff_dvd_digits_sum`. This subsumes all classical divisibility-by-digit-sum tests.
mathContext: If $d \mid (b-1)$, then $b \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$, so $n = \sum d_i b^i \equiv \sum d_i \pmod{d}$. Special cases: in base 10, $3 \mid 9$ gives div-by-3; in base 16, $3 \mid 15$ and $5 \mid 15$ give div-by-3 and div-by-5 for hex.
prerequisites: divisor of b-1 implies b ≡ 1 mod d

title: Hexadecimal (Base 16) Examples
content: Concrete verifications in base 16: $\text{dr}_{16}(15) = 15$ (single-digit fixed point), $\text{dr}_{16}(16) = 1$ (since $16 \equiv 1 \pmod{15}$), $\text{dr}_{16}(255) = 15$ (since $255 = 17 \times 15$). Also proves that $15 \mid n \iff 15 \mid \text{digitSum}_{16}(n)$ -- casting out fifteens in hexadecimal.
mathContext: In hex: $b - 1 = 15 = 3 \times 5$. So digit sums test divisibility by 3, 5, and 15. $\text{dr}_{16}(\text{0xFF}) = \text{dr}_{16}(255) = 15$ confirms $15 \mid 255$.

title: Octal and Base-7 Examples
content: Further concrete verifications: in octal, $\text{dr}_8(7) = 7$ and $\text{dr}_8(64) = 1$ (since $64 = 8^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{7}$), with the divisibility rule $7 \mid n \iff 7 \mid \text{digitSum}_8(n)$. In base 7: $\text{dr}_7(42) = 6$ (since $42 = 7 \times 6$) and $\text{dr}_7(43) = 1$ (since $43 \equiv 1 \pmod{6}$).
mathContext: Octal: $b-1 = 7$ (prime), so digit sums test only divisibility by 7. Base 7: $b-1 = 6 = 2 \times 3$, so digit sums test divisibility by 2, 3, and 6.
